newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Drama, not facts, cloud Russian precious metals.
newsitem.headline: Drama, not facts, cloud Russian precious metals.

text.p: Russia, whose reputation as a precious metals supplier to the world was never sterling pure, may find its image on platinum and palladium markets tainted by uncertainty over delays in supplies.
Reams of opinion but few hard facts have come to light since Moscow threw international precious metals markets into turmoil by delaying white metals shipments for half a year.

Russia resumed sporadic deliveries to its biggest customer, Japan, last month, after a six-month suspension that sent prices into the stratosphere and left everybody from car manufacturers to jewellers wondering if they should use other metals.
Analysts said on Friday the lack of clarity over what Russia -- the world's largest supplier of palladium and second largest of platinum -- was up to could sit for a while in consumers' memories.
"If the Russians wanted to sow confusion, they've done a pretty good job," said Tony Warwick-Ching of CRU International.

"Almaz used to have a fine reputation in terms of supply and pricing," he said, referring to Almazjuvelirexport, the state agency which exports precious metals. "But the attitude now may not be too complimentary, and some of it has to stick."
Theories abound for what is happening. They run as follows:

-International hedge funds have stockpiled large amounts of platinum and palladium and are squeezing markets. The privatisation of Russia's biggest white metals producer, Norilsk Nickel, has whetted the appetite of its owners to make money on metals exports instead of selling to the state at a discount.
-The finance ministry is battling the central bank for control over the multi-billion dollar exports. Almazjuvelirexport is battling the finance ministry. Norilsk is battling Almazjuvelirexport.

-The former state body in charge of the precious metals sector, Roskomdragmet, is trying to rise from the dead after being disbanded last year. Almazjuverlirexport, which no longer speaks to the press, is locked in a battle with the Kremlin. UBS is in a secret deal to swap white metals for Russian gold.

-Russia has metals but is holding back to boost prices. Russia is running out of metals after having sold them to raise money to bolster its costly transition from socialism to a market-style economy. Russia is in the midst of a Bolshevik-sized bureaucratic tangle after President Boris reshuffled the cabinet this spring.
Which theory you buy depends on whom you talk to.
"It's not Machiavelli, it's Murphy," offered precious metals analyst Andy Smith of UBS in London, one of the few analysts who does not subscribe to the dwindling stockpiles theory.
"What can go wrong has gone wrong. With the bureaucratic and political problems, the by-product has been disrupted supply."

Whatever the reasons, Russia's delays caused platinum to hit seven year highs of $497 an ounce, while its sister-metal palladium rushed to 17-year-highs of $240 per ounce. Whatever the theory, the outcome has been the same -- wary consumers.

"It (the delays) won't mean the Russian market will dry up -- it can't because of Russia's importance as a supplier," said Rhona O'Connell of T Hoare & Co. "But it's perfectly possible they'll be the supplier of last choice."
Moscow's precious metals deliveries to world markets have been sketchy at times in the past.
But Russia, which with South Africa accounts for the bulk of supplies, cannot be avoided, since it accounts for 60 percent of world palladium and 20 percent of world platinum needs.

Japanese traders, annoyed by Moscow's lack of clarity over when and how it plans to sell the metals, got some consolation on Friday when they reported the arrival of a Russian metals shipment for August under long-term contracts.
But drip-feeding will not be enough.

"There needs to be a pipeline filled pretty damn quick so normal, professional business in the forwards market can go ahead," Smith said. "To put it right, you would need a very generous, open-hearted approach to negotiations (for the next long-term contracts) -- something to reassure clients supplies will be consistent, and not hit-or-miss."
Other analysts also argued the need for clarity.
"Once they get these (bureacratic and political) issues sorted out, things will clearly settle down," said Warwick-Ching. "But they're clearly nowhere near this."
